lessons.title: Catalog, variants, and stock
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of identity of a sellable variant in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of identity of a sellable variant.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: A product groups content and marketing, while a variant represents the unit actually selected, priced, and stocked. A size-color combination therefore has its own identifier and stock; the interface must never reconstruct identity from fragile labels. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: identity of a sellable variant is like a control chain where every station verifies the receipt before passing the parcel onward. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

Product.id identifies the model and Variant.id the purchasable combination; the cart carries variantId so server and stock refer to the exact same row. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

Displayed stock guides selection but remains a snapshot that can change; only atomic checkout validation actually reserves an item. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

Images, labels, and color order may change without breaking orders because relationships use stable identifiers and snapshots. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Cart, quantities, and money
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of deterministic cart calculation in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of deterministic cart calculation.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: The client cart is an intent made of identifiers and quantities, not an authority over prices. Amounts remain integer cents throughout calculations and become a localized string only at the final display step. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: deterministic cart calculation is like a control chain where every station verifies the receipt before passing the parcel onward. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

One line per variantId merges repeated additions, bounds quantity between one and a reasonable limit, and removes the line when the user chooses removal. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

Subtotal, shipping, and total derive from lines; storing them separately would allow desynchronization when quantity changes. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

localStorage improves continuity but is editable: the server ignores client unitPriceCents and reloads every variant before validation. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.

blocks.text: Checkout collects intent and an address, then the server rebuilds truth from the database: variants, prices, stock, coupon, and shipping. An order and its historical lines are created in a transaction with an explicit state before payment. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: server-side order creation is like a control chain where every station verifies the receipt before passing the parcel onward. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

The API accepts variantId and quantity but ignores client name, price, and total; it requires every requested variant to exist and remain available. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

blocks.text: The browser may start payment, but only the provider confirms its result through a signed server notification. A webhook is delivered at least once, possibly late or out of order, so handling must verify signature, amount, currency, identity, and idempotency. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: reliable payment confirmation is like a control chain where every station verifies the receipt before passing the parcel onward. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

The signature is verified according to the provider protocol before trusting the body; knowing an orderId does not authorize marking it paid. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

event.id has a unique constraint: replay returns success without recreating email, points, stock decrement, or refund. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

Locking the order and comparing total/currency prevents concurrent events or a partial amount from producing an inconsistent transition. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
